subject: Core CPI is 1.8%. The Bank may hike anyway.
bodyMarkdown:
If you hold a variable mortgage or renew in the next few months, the Bank of Canada's December 9 decision is worth twelve days of your attention. Markets now put the odds of another quarter-point increase at about four in five, and the reason has almost nothing to do with the Canadian economy running hot.

## What Macklem actually said

CBC reported that Tiff Macklem, speaking to the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto on Tuesday, said businesses have absorbed most of the higher production and transport costs from this year's oil shock, and that he expects more of those costs to reach shoppers in 2027. What worries him is **second-round effects**, meaning one price increase feeding into wages and other prices instead of fading out. He also said something that cuts the other way. Oil prices and refinery margins have come down, and fourth-quarter inflation will probably land cooler than the Bank's own forecast. The Bank's October monetary policy report had inflation above 3 per cent for most of 2027. My read is that Macklem now thinks that forecast is too high for the next few months and too relaxed about next year.

## The economy underneath is not hot

Headline inflation was 3.1 per cent in October, unchanged from September, Statistics Canada reported earlier this month. Strip out energy and it was 2.0 per cent. **CPI-trim**, one of the Bank's two preferred core measures, which discards the most extreme price moves each month, eased to 1.8 per cent. Gasoline by itself was up 30.9 per cent from a year earlier. Nearly the entire gap above the 2 per cent target is energy. Meanwhile the real economy is soft. GDP stalled in August, StatCan's advance estimate had September real GDP down 0.1 per cent, and its October retail sales estimate fell 1.5 per cent in nominal terms. The one number pointing the other way arrived yesterday, when Statistics Canada reported average weekly earnings up 3.3 per cent over twelve months and 528,100 job vacancies in September, up 3.4 per cent from August.

## Why the Bank may move anyway

Higher rates do not make gasoline cheaper. They work by cooling demand, and demand is already cooling on its own. The case for December 9 is about expectations. If households and businesses start planning around 3 per cent as the normal rate of inflation, the Bank has to spend much more later to pull that back, and Macklem has been plain that this is the risk he cares about. Markets think he will act. Using LSEG data, pricing moved to roughly a 79 per cent chance of a quarter-point increase, up from 63 per cent a week earlier, and all of the big six banks now forecast a hike. CIBC's chief economist read the speech's focus on lingering inflation risk as a sign the Bank is preparing a second straight increase. The October 28 move took the policy rate to 2.50 per cent and lifted bank prime from 4.45 to 4.70 per cent.

## The takeaway

If you are on a variable rate, do the arithmetic on a 2.75 per cent policy rate and prime at 4.95 per cent before the decision, not after it. Ratehub's example for the October hike was about $82 more a month on a $666,538 mortgage, so a second quarter point is roughly another $80. I would not lock into a long fixed term on the strength of twelve days of market pricing, partly because Macklem himself said near-term inflation is coming in below forecast, and that is exactly the kind of thing that changes a vote. Watch CPI-trim and CPI-median: if they sit near 1.8 and 2.0 per cent, then a December increase is the Bank protecting its credibility on expectations, and the economy itself does not need the cooling.
